name: Tsunami
label: Simple Machines
lede: Jenny Toomey and Kristin Thomson ran a record label from their Arlington living room, started a band for a New Year's party, and toured it for seven years. They closed both in 1998; a box set pulled Tsunami back out of the archive 26 years later.

eras.title: A party band goes on tour
eras.text: Toomey and Thomson were housemates in a Positive Force house in Arlington, Virginia, and already running Simple Machines from it. The band was a party plan; by February it was in a van opening for Beat Happening.

years.cap: Tsunami hanging off a federal building in Washington, D.C.
years.h: Two housemates start a band for a New Year's party
years.p: [[Jenny Toomey|246fc8dd-a667-4a5b-868a-a5897bcd6c59]] and [[Kristin Thomson|a7a793e4-d41c-4286-a494-03a31305b4bc]], who run Simple Machines from a Positive Force house in Arlington, recruit drummer John Pamer and bassist Andrew Webster, late of the band Bricks.
years.xp: The Positive Force house was a communal home tied to a DC activist group, and Washingtonian calls it the band's birthplace. Wikipedia says Tsunami started late in 1990 with the party in mind.

years.h: The first show lands before the songs do
years.p: The band's bio says the first show was planned for January 1991, before the four had practiced seriously.

years.cap: Opening for Beat Happening in an attic in Milwaukee, 1991
years.h: On tour with Beat Happening, the transmission quits in Indiana
years.p: Weeks after the first show, Tsunami heads across the country supporting [[Beat Happening|449e44cb-bcae-4c48-a1af-5d8df0f81456]]. The van dies at 2 a.m., and the band loses two days in a hotel before it reaches Milwaukee.
years.xp:
The breakdown comes from the band's own bio, which dates the tour to February 1991 and the Milwaukee date to the other side of that hotel stay.

The bio also lists a Cow Arcade demo from March 1991, the first recordings to come out of the tour.

years.big: "We had to be in a tent because there were fleas everywhere!"
years.h: Tsunami sleeps in a tent inside Olympia's Capitol Theater
years.p: Toomey on the International Pop Underground Convention in Olympia, where Tsunami played a bill with [[Bikini Kill|1397d045-1603-41fc-80b9-712c18360145]], [[Fugazi|233fc3f3-6de2-465c-985e-e721dbabbace]] and Thee Headcoats.
years.xp:
The band set the tent up in the aisle of the theater. Toomey told WNYU's Static that the recycling room was the obvious second choice, but everybody else had had the same idea, so they ended up in someone's yard, where the fleas followed.

It happened weeks before Nevermind came out.

years.h: Eight weeks after Olympia, Simple Machines throws its own festival
years.p: Lots of Pop Losers fills two days in DC, October 26 and 27, with 14 bands, booked by mail and phone.
years.xp:
Thomson laid out the timing for WNYU's Static: "that's like eight weeks later. And this is pre-Internet!"

Tsunami was one of the acts at the label's own party.

eras.title: Deep End waits, then the road takes over
eras.text: A debut album stalled at the pressing plant for ten months, a Lollapalooza side stage and roughly 150 other shows filled 1993, and a second album followed on the road.

years.h: Velocity Girl and Tsunami split a seven-inch for Sub Pop
years.p: Velocity Girl, from Maryland, takes the other side; the single carries Tsunami past the Simple Machines catalog.
years.xp: Wikipedia lists the Sub Pop split, 1992, among the singles Tsunami put out before its first album.

years.cap: Toomey, Thomson, Pamer and Webster on the Georgetown campus, c. 1992
years.h: Deep End gets recorded in summer, then waits ten months
years.p: The band cuts its first album in summer 1992. Manufacturing problems hold the pressing until early 1993.
years.xp: The ten-month figure is from Tsunami's bio; Wikipedia blames manufacturing delays too. Video survives of a Fort Reno set in DC from 1992.

years.h: Deep End finally arrives on Simple Machines
years.p: Two singers, interlocking guitars and a run of seven-inches behind it. By May the band is in front of John Peel.
years.xp: The Washington Post and the band's press pages file the sound under math rock, Riot Grrrl and a little twee, built on the label's DIY habits.

years.cap: Pamer, Webster, Toomey and Thomson on the Georgetown campus, c. 1993
years.h: Tsunami works Lollapalooza's side stage, plus about 150 other shows
years.p: Six side-stage dates alongside [[Sebadoh|d98c8149-0c01-4151-93e1-48fdc3d5027f]], [[Free Kitten|7e623dd5-bf40-4f8b-ba71-8226afc918e2]] and [[Thurston Moore|8ba48525-d922-42ee-9775-97b7b8f9712e]].
years.xp:
Thomson, on 1993, to WNYU's Static: "We played Lollapalooza shows, but also we played like another 150 shows." The second album was being made in between.

Back at the office, Simple Machines was running its Working Holiday record club: a split seven-inch every month for about 800 members.

years.h: Album two, The Heart's Tremolo, comes out of the van
years.p: Written and recorded while the band toured hard. Two US tours, an English tour and a Phoenix Festival slot followed.
years.xp: Wikipedia counts the two US tours and the English one after the record, with Phoenix on the Melody Maker Stage.

years.h: Tsunami lands on the Working Holiday! compilation
years.p: The label's compilation ties into the record club that sent a split seven-inch to about 800 members each month.
years.xp: Thomson gave the 800 figure to WNYU's Static, along with the club's rule: one new split every month.

eras.title: A drummer goes to college
eras.text: Tsunami kept putting out singles while its founding rhythm section drifted off. A split with Superchunk, one drummer's year at UMass Amherst and a new drummer set up the last album.

years.h: World Tour & Other Destinations gathers the singles
years.p: The band's seven-inches in one place, listed by Wikipedia as a Simple Machines release.

years.h: Superchunk and Tsunami split a seven-inch on Honeybear
years.p: Wikipedia dates the single to 1995, on the Honeybear label.

years.h: John Pamer takes a year off at UMass Amherst
years.p: The drummer steps away to study; the band's bio calls it a hiatus.

years.h: Luther Gray takes the drums; Webster and Pamer are out
years.p: Pamer graduates and moves on to New York City. Arlington drummer Luther Gray steps in.
years.xp: Wikipedia says Gray came aboard after six months of rehearsals. Tsunami's bio dates the departures of Andrew Webster and John Pamer to 1996.

eras.title: A Brilliant Mistake, then the lights go off
eras.text: The last album was made in Chicago with a bigger lineup. In 1998 Toomey and Thomson closed Simple Machines and let the band go with it.

years.h: A Brilliant Mistake gets made at Kingsize Soundlabs in Chicago
years.p: Gray plays drums on it, and Amy Domingues and Bob Massey join for the tour.
years.xp: Wikipedia puts the release in August 1997, on Simple Machines.

years.h: Amy Domingues and Bob Massey fill out the last lineup
years.p: Domingues plays bass and cello, Massey guitar and keyboards; the bio dates both to 1997 and 1998.

years.cap: Thomson, Gray, Massey, Webster, Toomey and Domingues at the Simple Machines Finale party, Washington, D.C., 1998
years.h: Simple Machines closes with a party, and Tsunami plays it
years.p: Toomey and Thomson shut a label that put out nearly 80 releases, then play the finale.
years.xp:
The bio dates the party to March 1998, after which Tsunami stopped regular activity. Wikipedia says the band disbanded that year after a final East Coast tour.

The label's 24-page Mechanics Guide to Putting Out Records had gone out to would-be label owners, including future Numero Group co-founder Ken Shipley. Thomson: "Ken was one of the recipients, and he still has his Mechanics Guide."

eras.title: Ladyfests and the Future of Music
eras.text: Toomey and Thomson turned the label's habits into policy work, and Tsunami showed up only for the occasional set.

years.h: Toomey and Thomson turn to policy at the Future of Music Coalition
years.p: Toomey becomes executive director and Thomson education director of the advocacy group, per Wikipedia. The Creative Independent says Tsunami also played a handful of shows in 2000.

years.h: Two Ladyfest sets, in Washington and Philadelphia
years.p: Between 2001 and 2003 Toomey and Thomson play with former members and guests in both cities.

eras.title: Loud Is As
eras.text: Numero Group dug the band out of the archive, and Tsunami, with a new rhythm section, went back on the road.

years.h: Tsunami returns at Numero Twenty in Los Angeles
years.p: After 25 years, the band plays Numero Group's festival, with a new rhythm section: Rob Christiansen on bass and Franklin Bruno on guitar and keyboards.
years.xp: The lineup is Toomey, Thomson, Luther Gray, Christiansen and Bruno. The festival came alongside Numero's reissue project.

years.h: Numero Group packs the singles, demos and three albums into five LPs
years.p: Loud Is As has 61 songs and a book of essays and photos; The Big Takeover called it a marvel of physical preservation.
years.xp:
Washingtonian gives November 8, 2024 as the release; the Inquirer says October. The set remasters three of the four albums. Toomey told WNYU's Static the box used only about 2 percent of the journals, letters and flyers they kept.

Wikipedia reports best-of-year placement at the New York Times and Billboard, and a Grammy nomination for Best Recording Package at the 2026 awards. It lost to Bruce Springsteen's Tracks II: The Lost Albums.

years.cap: Coin Toss Tour poster, Tsunami and Ida, c. 2025
years.h: Tsunami and Ida flip a coin every night to decide who opens
years.p: The Coin Toss Tour hits the Black Cat in DC on March 27 and Underground Arts in Philadelphia on March 28.
years.xp:
Kate Pierson of the B-52s sat in at the Woodstock show, and the Inquirer expected more guests in Philadelphia, where tickets were $29.50. Thomson and Toomey stepped away from their jobs for six months to do it.

Toomey to the Inquirer: "It is a weird moment politically to be coming back with everything feeling as precarious as it does."

Washingtonian and the Inquirer each call their city the tour's first show, so the real opener is unclear.
